question: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of severe, acute, right leg pain for 2 hours. The patient's symptoms started suddenly while he was doing household chores. He has no history of leg pain at rest or with exertion. Yesterday, he returned home after a 6-hour bus ride from his grandson's home. He has hypertension treated with ramipril. He appears uncomfortable. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 105/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg. The right lower extremity is cool and tender to touch. A photograph of the limb is shown. Femoral pulses are palpable bilaterally; popliteal and pedal pulses are decreased on the right side. Sensation to pinprick and light touch and muscle strength are decreased in the right lower extremity. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying source of this patient's condition?

enhanced_information: The 72-year-old man presents with acute right leg pain, coolness, tenderness, and decreased pulses, indicating acute limb ischemia likely due to embolism or thrombosis, especially after prolonged immobility. Doppler ultrasonography is the most appropriate initial test to assess blood flow and identify occlusion in the affected leg. While echocardiography can identify potential cardiac sources of embolism, it is less direct for limb assessment. Digital subtraction angiography, although useful for visualizing blood vessels, is invasive and not first-line for acute assessment. Therefore, Doppler ultrasonography is the best option to confirm the underlying source of this patient's condition.
analysis: The patient's presentation is highly suggestive of acute limb ischemia, likely due to an embolism or thrombosis, especially given the sudden onset of severe pain, coolness, and decreased pulses in the right leg. To confirm the underlying source of this condition, Doppler ultrasonography of the legs is the most appropriate initial imaging modality. It can assess blood flow and identify any occlusions or abnormalities in the arterial supply. While echocardiography could help identify a cardiac source of emboli, it does not directly assess the leg's vascular status. Digital subtraction angiography is more invasive and typically used for therapeutic interventions rather than initial diagnosis. Therefore, the best option to confirm the underlying source of this patient's condition is Doppler ultrasonography of the legs.
